rules.stmt: Boundary choice moves a hotel's per-night footprint more than property choice does: adding purchased food, waste and laundry to a Scope 1+2 inventory raises a full-service room-night by 70-130%, so the same hotel can sit anywhere between roughly 9 and 56 kgCO2e per room-night depending on what is counted.
ev: Attari & Hanrahan 2026 (preprint, four Irish hotels, 3- to 5-star): Scope 1+2 only 9.40 / 16.59 / 25.10 / 32.32 kgCO2e per room-night; full Scope 1-3 (food procurement, food waste, landfill, recycling) 15.87 / 40.30 / 47.15 / 56.14; the authors' own section 5.

Filimonau et al. 2011 (two UK 3-star hotels, full text): operational 7.5 and 4.5 kgCO2e per guest-night; adding breakfast (1.3 kg), daily laundry (1.75 kg) and a 15% embodied uplift gives 11.65 and 8.25, a 55-83% increase (own arithmetic on the paper's figures

Morales et al. 2026 (Beijing five-star): 95.9 kgCO2e per guest-night under an extended operational boundary vs 36.7 from the Greenview HFT benchmark for the same property class, a 2.6x spread from boundary alone.

rules.stmt: Once purchased food and drink are inside the boundary they are the largest single category of a full-service hotel's footprint, at 40-58% of a room-night, and the share rises as the electricity grid gets cleaner.
ev: Attari & Hanrahan 2026: food and beverage procurement 43.2% / 57.7% / 43.1% / 39.7% of total at the four hotels, "the single largest emission category at every property".

Dolder Grand: Food & Beverages 1,713.9 of 3,541.9 t (48%, 2023), 52% (2024), 2,257.7 of 4,047.5 t (56%, 2025), against purchased electricity 3-4% and heating/cooling 11-12% on Zurich's hydro-nuclear grid.

Accor URD 2024 (group, worldwide, via Projet Celsius): catering and drinks 19% (1,229 kt) vs energy 65% (4,282 kt); the same source states that in a French hotel on low-carbon electricity "energy weighs less and catering more".

rules.stmt: Energy-only (HCMI-basis) footprints for luxury hotels in the United States and Western Europe cluster at 20-50 kgCO2e per occupied room-night; in Asia and the Gulf the same metric runs 50-95.
ev: CHSB 2025 (CY2023, location-based eGRID factors): NYC luxury non-resort median 28.39 (n=21, IQR 23.95-38.19); US luxury 32.12 (n=137, IQR 25.08-43.62); US 5-star 36.04; US luxury Measure 3 (whole hotel, no apportionment) 32.19.
CHSB 2025 cross-country luxury medians: UK 23.34, Canada 20.56, Spain 17.65, France 15.60, Germany 33.29, US 32.12; India 84.01, UAE 68.52, China 66.64, Japan 52.13, Singapore 36.19.
Huang, Wang & Wang 2015 (58 Taiwanese luxury hotels, abstract verified): 50 kgCO2e per room-night sold, 29 per guest-night, 132 kgCO2e/m2/yr.

rules.stmt: The normalising denominator changes a hotel's ranking: per occupied room-night, per guest-night and per square metre give different orderings, and per-guest-night values are roughly half of per-room-night values in full-service hotels.
ev: Xuchao, Priyadarsini & Lee 2010 (Singapore, abstract verified): "a hotel's carbon intensity ranking is rather sensitive to the normalizing denominator chosen."

CHSB 2025 (CY2023): NYC luxury is lower than US luxury per occupied room (28.39 vs 32.12) but higher per m2 of conditioned space (88.68 vs 83.83 kgCO2e/m2) and in energy per m2 (321.61 vs 300.70 kWh/m2), because NYC properties are high-rise with less area per
CHSB 2025: US luxury is 2.3x upper-midscale per occupied room (32.12 vs 14.03) but 1.43x per m2 (83.83 vs 58.77).

rules.stmt: The luxury premium is 2.3-3.1x midscale per occupied room-night but only 1.4-1.5x per square metre, so roughly 60% of the per-room-night gap is floor area per occupied room (bigger rooms, more public and back-of-house space, lower occupancy) and about 40% is higher intensity per square metre.
ev: CHSB 2025 (CY2023, US, Measure 3): luxury 32.19 vs upper midscale 12.62 (2.55x) and midscale 10.24 (3.1x); Measure 1: 32.12 vs 14.03 (2.3x) and 11.74 (2.7x). Per m2 (Measure 4): 83.83 vs 58.77 (1.43x). kWh per occupied room 119.35 vs 42.20 (2.83x); kWh/m2 300.

Brighter Planet 2012: "A hotel with 80 square feet of floor space per room consumes more than three times as much energy per room-night as a hotel with 20"; the average upscale hotel uses 25% more energy per room-night than the average budget hotel; square foo
CHSB 2023 outlier screens: full-service luxury accepted at 50-700 kWh per occupied room, midscale at 20-300, i.e. the benchmark's authors expect about 2x.

rules.stmt: Occupancy inverts star-rating rankings in per-night metrics: a 2-star hotel at 30% occupancy out-emits a 5-star at 50%, pooled occupancy is not a significant predictor of total energy and turns negative for upscale hotels, and a 10-point occupancy swing moves per-room-night intensity by 10-25%.
ev: Puig et al. 2017 (full text): 2-star 23, 5-star 22, 4-star 12 kgCO2e per overnight stay at 30%, 50% and 90-100% occupancy; the authors call the footprint "inversely proportional to the occupancy rate".
Arenhart et al. 2024: pooled correlation of occupancy with energy use 0.20, not significant; 0.36 for general hotels, -0.21 for upscale.

CHSB trend: NYC luxury 40.54 kgCO2e per occupied room in CY2021 (pandemic recovery, n=8) against 21.78 (CY2019) and 26.19 (CY2022); US luxury resorts 56.07 in CY2021; CHSB 2024 reports energy per m2 -9.59% but energy per occupied room +9.26% across all hotels

rules.stmt: Area-based apportionment (HCMI, CHSB Measure 1, Hilton LightStay) gives every room-night the same footprint whether or not the guest used the spa, pool or restaurant, removes only about 5% from rooms in NYC luxury hotels, and no large benchmarking regression carries an amenity term.
ev: HCMI v2.0 sec 6.3-7.2: all remaining areas "of heart of house, spa, retail, fitness, public space, restaurants, etc." are "allocated proportionately to Rooms and Meeting Space"; "The methodology assumes equal intensity for all areas of the hotel"; "each occupi
CHSB 2025 NYC luxury: Measure 1 (rooms, area-apportioned) 28.39 vs Measure 3 (whole hotel per occupied room) 27.02; US luxury 32.12 vs 32.19, so the meeting-space apportionment moves rooms by 0-5%.
CHSB 2025 report: "no additional information was collected on the range of amenities that could contribute towards hotels' utility use"; CHSB 2018 and 2023 state amenities cannot be accounted for.

rules.stmt: The electricity emission factor chosen moves a New York hotel's energy-only footprint by 36-50%, more than any single operational intervention measured in the evidence base.
ev: eGRID2023 NYCW total output rate 864.5 lb CO2/MWh = 0.392 kgCO2e/kWh (location-based, Portfolio Manager, CHSB); LL97 prescribed coefficient 0.000288962 tCO2e/kWh = 0.289 for 2024-29 (36% lower); LL97 2030-34 coefficient 0.000145 = 0.145 (50% below 2024-29, 63%
Portfolio Manager's embedded eGRID factor itself moved from 81.4 kgCO2e/MBtu (CY2013) to 92.8 (CY2016) to 73.8 (CY2021) in the Waldorf's LL84 filings, a 14-26% swing with no change in the building.
CHSB trend: US luxury HCMI median fell 26% CY2016-CY2018 (43.30 to 31.97) while kWh per occupied room fell 9% (143.96 to 131.28); the difference is grid factor and sample.

rules.stmt: Per-square-metre intensity targets can be met while absolute emissions rise: every major chain reporting a per-m2 or per-room reduction of 11-51% since its base year also reports absolute emissions flat or up, by 8-84%.
ev: Hilton 2025 Performance Tables (DEKRA-assured): managed Scope 1+2 intensity -50.9% vs 2008 (0.1567 to 0.0769 tCO2e/m2) while absolute market-based managed Scope 1+2 rose from 2,229,587 to 2,443,342 tCO2e (+9.6%) and franchised Scope 3 from 2,180,912 to 4,011,3

IHG Annual Report 2025: carbon per available room -11.0% vs 2019 (0.0297 to 0.0258 tCO2e) while "total carbon emissions are up 7.7% since 2019"; IHG self-declares off track against its validated absolute -46.2% target.
Mandarin Oriental 2023: carbon intensity per m2 -22% vs 2012 while absolute Scope 1+2 rose as floor area more than doubled from 574,935 m2.

rules.stmt: Offset-based "carbon-neutral stay" claims have failed scientifically (6-94% of credits non-additional in the project types hotels buy) and legally (courts in three jurisdictions and an EU per se ban from 27 September 2026), and the one hotel ruling turned on an omitted amenity boundary.
ev: West et al. 2023 (Science 381:873-877): only 6.1% of credits from 18 REDD+ projects were linked to additional reductions; 68% came from projects that did not significantly reduce deforestation (Verra disputes the method).

Badgley et al. 2022 (GCB): California forest offsets over-credited by 29.4% (30.0 MtCO2e, 90% CI 20.5-38.6); Coffield et al. 2022: 37 IFM projects "generally not additional"; Haya et al. 2023: IFM protocols "deviate from scientific understanding".
ICVCM (15 Nov 2024): CCP label for three new REDD+ methodologies only; legacy Verra methodologies that "account for the majority of REDD+ credits on the market" excluded.

rules.stmt: Water heating is the largest single end use in US lodging at about 20% of site energy (16.5 kBtu/ft2 in 2018, 24.2 in 2012) and about half of a full-service hotel's gas; only HVAC taken as a whole exceeds it.
ev: EIA CBECS 2018 Table E2 (lodging, kBtu/ft2): water heating 16.5, space heating 15.7, cooking 14.1, ventilation 12.5, lighting 7.2, cooling 6.0, refrigeration 4.2 of 85.7 total; CBECS 2012: water heating 24.2 of 96.9, the largest end use by a wider margin.

PNNL/ACEEE 2010 (300+ room full-service hotel, Washington DC area, 2009): service hot water 51% of natural gas (~27,900 therms/yr, about 7.5 kWh thermal per available room-day, notes' arithmetic), kitchen ~25%, laundry ~25%.
EPA WaterSense: heating water needs 0.183 kWh per gallon = 0.048 kWh per litre for a 41.7 K rise, before heater efficiency; water heating is ~90% of a clothes washer's energy.

rules.stmt: Among wellness amenities only heated water (pools, hydrotherapy, thermal suites) carries a load of the same order as guestroom HVAC and hot water; treatment rooms, gyms and their equipment each add well under 1 kgCO2e per room-night.
ev: Borowski et al. 2022 (Hotel Turówka, Kraków, 51 rooms, 4,620 m2, heat-metered): pool-area heating 399.6 (June) to 657.4 kWh/day (May), peak 63.7 kWh/h, against domestic hot water 299.4-1,573.6 kWh/day; annualised lower bound 146-240 MWh/yr = 32-52 kWh per m2 o
Attari & Hanrahan 2026: the 5-star spa/pool property's electricity (333 tCO2e) was ten times the city 4-star's (32 t).

CIBSE TM46:2008 (per m2 floor, per year): swimming pool centre 245 electricity + 1,130 fossil = 1,375 kWh/m2 vs hotel 105 + 330 = 435 and fitness & health centre 160 + 440 = 600 (secondary reproduction).

rules.stmt: Pool-facility energy scales with bathers and water throughput, not primarily with climate, and evaporation is 46-60% or more of pool-water heat loss; the right allocation key for a hotel pool is visits or m2 of water surface, not degree-days or floor area.
ev: Kampel et al. 2016 (43 Norwegian facilities, 176 datasets, abstract verified): "Unlike in residential and commercial buildings, climate does not drive the total energy performance of swimming facilities. Instead, overall water usage of the facility was observe
Nitter et al. (NTNU survey, 37 facilities, 2017 data, climate-corrected): bather load and opening days explain ~77% of energy (adjusted R2 0.77, n=30); 6.7-35 kWh per bather.
Borowski et al. 2022 (Kraków hotel): correlation between pool-area heating demand and outdoor temperature "low" in summer; occupancy explained more of DHW.

rules.stmt: A beef-centred main carries 8-11 times the footprint of a vegetarian main, and a luxury-hotel restaurant cover runs 5.4-6.6 kgCO2e, about three times a global-average meal and above the WRI Cool Food lunch/dinner threshold of 5.38.
ev: Danish meal-service LCA (Int. J. LCA 2018): average main 3.70 kgCO2e; veal/beef mains 5-7x the average of other meals and 8-11x the average vegetarian meal.

Poore & Nemecek 2018 (OWID, kgCO2e/kg): beef-herd beef 99.48, dairy-herd beef 33.3, lamb 39.72, cheese 23.88, poultry 9.87, eggs 4.67, vegetables ~0.5; Clune et al. 2017 medians: beef 28.73 (10.74-109.5), lamb 27.91, cheese 8.86, chicken 4.12, field vegetables
Dolder Grand: 5.9 (2023), 5.4 (2024), 6.1 (2025) kgCO2e per restaurant guest; Accor 2023: 1.66-6.57 kgCO2e per meal.

rules.stmt: Hotel food waste runs 0.3-0.5 kg per cover with buffets two to three times à la carte, and kitchens that weigh it cut it about 21% within a year at a benefit-cost ratio near 7:1.
ev: Papargyropoulou et al. 2019 (five Malaysian operations incl. a five-star hotel restaurant and a high-end banquet hall): 0.53 kg food waste per customer average; the hotel restaurant produced over eight times the least wasteful site; the banquet hall prepared 3

Camilleri-Fenech et al. 2020 (Malta five-star, one month): plate waste buffet dinner 0.48 kg/person vs à la carte dinner 0.16 and lunch 0.21; preparation waste 0.08 kg/person; removing the side plate cut plate waste from 0.059 to 0.043 kg.
EPA Ireland benchmarks (search-summary only): ~360 g per cover daily service, ~530 g per cover for functions; buffet breakfast 300 g vs plated 130 g (unsourced).

rules.stmt: Linen laundry adds about 6-10 kWh and 2-3 kgCO2e per occupied room-night at a full-service hotel (5-7 kg of linen at 1.6-1.7 kWh/kg and about 0.4 kgCO2 per kg), a figure corroborated by one hotel's own opt-out sign.
ev: Linen mass: 5-8 kg per occupied room-day when sheets, pillowcases, towels and robes are changed (Clean Group); 10-15 lb (4.5-6.8 kg) (Hospitality Institute); 12 lb (5.4 kg) for a full-service hotel with pool and banquets (Hotel Management 2021); observed range

Energy and carbon per kg: TRSA 2018 (132 US plants) 2,422 Btu/lb = 1.57 kWh/kg and 0.413 lb CO2/lb = 0.41 kgCO2/kg, water 12.3 L/kg; UK trade benchmark 1.6-1.7 kWh/kg typical, 0.8-1.0 attainable; TRSA Clean Green thresholds 1.94-2.39 kWh/kg.
6 kg x 1.65 kWh/kg = 10 kWh and 6 kg x 0.41 = 2.5 kgCO2e per room-night (own arithmetic); at best practice (1.0 kWh/kg) ~6 kWh.

rules.stmt: Guest-behaviour and room-control levers each save at most 1-2 kgCO2e per occupied room-night (under 10% of an energy-only luxury night); signage is cheap, hardware is not, and vendor claims of 33-50% do not survive controlled measurement.
ev: DOE/PNNL 2012 (six Marriott-brand hotels, five vendors): occupancy-based guestroom HVAC controls saved 10.8-26.5% of guestroom HVAC energy (mean 18.4%), 167-589 kWh per room per year, at US$345-426 installed per room with simple paybacks of 5.3-17.9 years; per

UC Davis / SDG&E: "an analysis of all data combined does not show a statistically significant savings due to the control technology"; BPA Grouse Mountain Lodge: savings below comparable studies because of manual override; vendor claims of 33% (Verde/Wyndham, 2
Towel cards: +9 to +12 percentage points of reuse in the US (Goldstein et al. 2008); baseline cultural differences (US ~35% vs Germany 64% with no message) dwarf the signage effect.

rules.stmt: Luxury hotels use 500-800 litres of water per occupied room-night, two to five times the 140 L European frontrunner benchmark and about 1.5-2x the all-hotel average; the premium exists per room but not per square metre, and one large review finds no quality effect at all.
ev: Marriott managed portfolio: 0.788 m3 (788 L) per occupied room in 2022 (0.880 in 2021, 1.005 in 2020, 0.841 in 2016; 0.763 in 2023).
Ecologic 2007 / Hamele & Eckardt 2006 (via Ramazanova et al. 2021): average hotel 394 L per overnight stay, five-star 594 L; ~600 L/night in Moroccan five-star hotels (Eurostat 2009, secondary).

Puig et al. 2017 (primary): 0.58 / 0.32 / 0.19 / 0.54 m3 per overnight stay for 5* / 4* / 3* / 2* Spanish hotels; Morote et al. 2018: 520 L/tourist/day in 5-star vs 287 in 1-star; Olcina et al. 2016: 225.9 (5-star) to 127.87 L (2-star).

rules.stmt: The operating phase is 70-90% of a hotel's life-cycle energy and emissions, so a 10-20% uplift on operational figures bounds embodied and amenity-production carbon for an existing building.
ev: Rosselló-Batle et al. 2010 (Balearic hotels, 50-year life cycle, abstract verified): operating phase 70-80% of total energy use; materials manufacture about one fifth; electricity the main CO2 source. The author's 2016 thesis states 80-90% of life-cycle CO2 (s
Filimonau et al. 2011 (full text): non-operational (embodied) energy taken as 15% of operational for two UK hotels (1.1 and 0.7 kgCO2e per guest-night on 7.5 and 4.5 operational).

Taiwanese life-cycle study (repository record): 147.93 kgCO2e per standard room-night whole life cycle, with production and transport of amenities plus laundry ~16% of total and energy the main source.

rules.stmt: Dry in-room and building services (minibar, elevators, ice, dishwashing, toiletries, bottled water) each add under 1 kgCO2e per occupied room-night, but a single chauffeured airport transfer (8-13 kgCO2e one way in a luxury diesel or petrol car) can exceed the room's entire Scope 1+2 footprint for the night, and no hotel group reports it.
ev: Minibars: Dometic HiPro absorption units 0.53-0.70 kWh per 24 h (236-265 kWh/yr, EN 62552-3), compressor units about a third of that; 0.1-0.3 kgCO2e per occupied room-night on typical grids (notes' arithmetic); ~70% of travellers never use one, so energy per t

Elevators: 141 kWh/day at the 12-storey, 300+ room PNNL hotel, ~1% of electricity, ~0.47 kWh per room-day; CIBSE worked examples 0.038-0.27 kWh per cycle with 200-900 W standby; a medium-usage hotel lift at 300 trips/day ~47 kWh/day (notes' arithmetic). No hig
Ice 3.6-5.6 kWh per 100 lb (~0.02 kWh per 200 g serve); dishwashers 0.17-0.61 kWh per rack of 16-36 glasses (ENERGY STAR listings).

hyps.title: Electrify heat before buying RECs; a story that does them in the other order pays more cumulative LL97 penalty 2030-2040.
hyps.test: Story A: heat pumps replace the eight gas boilers in 2028, Zone J RECs purchased from 2030 for residual electricity; Story B: RECs from 2026 (CHPE available 2026), heat pumps in 2033. Same demand path. Metric: cumulative tCO2e (LL97 basis) and cumulative penalty dollars 2025-2040; also banked beneficial-electrification credit.
hyps.expected: A wins. RECs deduct only from electricity emissions (1 RCNY 103-14 (e)(1)), so in B the gas Scope 1 is untouched until 2033; the marginal coefficient for beneficial-electrification credit falls from 0.247 (2024) to 0.114 (2029), so A banks more credit; DOB says RECs cost more than the penalty after 2030, so B's early RECs are the expensive instrument. Refuted if B wins, which would mean REC price and the CHPE-era REC supply dominate, and the capital-timing knob should be examined.

hyps.title: Gas-side demand measures keep their carbon value through 2040; electric-side measures lose half of it in 2030. Sequence DHW, laundry and kitchen hot-water efficiency before guestroom HVAC controls.
hyps.test: Introduce 1 GWh/yr of saving as (i) gas in 2026, (ii) electricity in 2026, (iii) gas in 2032, (iv) electricity in 2032. Metric: cumulative tCO2e 2025-2040 per GWh saved.
hyps.expected: (i) ≈ (iii) ≈ 0.181 kg/kWh x years; (ii) falls from 0.289 to 0.145 kg/kWh at 2030; electric saving is worth about half as much carbon after 2030. PNNL: service hot water is 51% of hotel gas and laundry about 25% (note 04 KQ1). Refuted only if the Storyline's gas coefficient path falls, which the rule text does not provide for.

hyps.title: One opted-out housekeeping night saves 2-5 times the carbon of one occupancy-controlled room-night today and 4-10 times in 2030, so opt-in housekeeping outranks HVAC controls as a guest-facing lever.
hyps.test: Opt-out night at the Sheraton Boston values (37.2 gal water, 0.19 kWh electricity, 25,000 BTU = 7.33 kWh gas); OBC at the DOE/PNNL 18.4% of guestroom HVAC (0.9-2.6 kWh per occupied room-night). Metric: kgCO2e per room-night per measure under 2024-29 and 2030-34 coefficients.
hyps.expected: opt-out 7.33 x 0.181 + 0.19 x 0.289 = 1.38 kg (1.35 kg in 2030); OBC 0.26-0.75 kg (0.13-0.38 in 2030). Supported if the ratio is in those ranges. Refuted if the Studio's laundry module gives much lower gas per opted-out night; luxury linen at 12-25 lb per room should push the other way. Uptake is unknown (no Hilton or Marriott opt-in rates found) and must be a Monte Carlo range.

hyps.title: Procurement before kitchen: a cut in the meat share of food carbon beats full kitchen electrification on the full-scope guest-night in every year, and has zero effect on LL97 exposure.
hyps.test: Story A: meat share of food carbon from 27% (Accor) to half that (assumption knob) in 2026; Story B: all kitchen gas (CBECS cooking 14.1 kBtu/ft2, 10.1 of it gas) to electric induction in 2026. Metrics: full-scope kgCO2e per guest-night; LL97 tCO2e.
hyps.expected: A moves the full-scope night by several kg (food is 40-58% of it; Dolder 5.4-6.1 kg per restaurant guest); B moves it by well under 1 kg per cover (kitchen energy 0.5-1.5 kgCO2e per cover inferred in note 03) and reduces LL97 emissions by the gas-to-electric delta. The hypothesis is that the two lever sets are disjoint: A is invisible to LL97, B is nearly invisible to the full-scope night. Refuted if B's full-scope effect approaches A's, which would mean the Studio's kitchen energy per cover is far above Mudie's 1.5-3.3 kWh.

hyps.title: Retire the CHP in 2030: a story that keeps the 555 kW CHP running after 2030 has higher LL97 emissions than one that buys grid electricity, unless heat utilisation exceeds a threshold the Storyline can compute.
hyps.test: CHP asset with electrical-efficiency knob (sweep 0.30-0.45), heat-utilisation knob (0-100% of recoverable heat displacing boiler gas at 0.201 kg/kWh heat), 6,000 h/yr (assumption). Metric: net LL97 tCO2e versus a no-CHP story, 2025-29 and 2030-34.
hyps.expected: before 2030 the CHP is near break-even only with high heat utilisation; after 2030 it loses at every efficiency in the sweep unless heat utilisation is high, because 0.181/e exceeds 0.145 for all e below 1.25 (I7). Refuted if the Storyline's LL97 CHP credit (mechanics not researched) is large enough to flip the sign; that would be a finding about the rule, not the plant.

hyps.title: The full-scope multiplier on the Waldorf's energy-only night is below the Irish 1.7-2.4 under the 2024-29 LL97 factor and rises toward it under the 2030 factor, with no change in the food knobs.
hyps.test: Fix food, laundry, waste at defaults; vary electricity factor 0.392, 0.289, 0.145. Metric: full-scope / Scope 1+2 ratio.
hyps.expected: the ratio falls as the factor rises (I1); Zurich (electricity 3-4% of total) is the limit case. Supported if the ratio spans roughly 1.4-2.2 across the three factors; refuted if it is flat, which would mean the Studio's food line is small relative to the notes' 5-6 kg per cover.

hyps.title: The Waldorf exceeds the CHSB NYC luxury upper quartile (38.19) per occupied room-night at any hotel GFA per key above about 950 ft2, while sitting at the Manhattan luxury peer median per m2.
hyps.test: Fix intensity at 11.3 kgCO2e/ft2 (122 kg/m2) and occupancy at 76.4%; sweep GFA per key 800-2,700 ft2. Metric: kg per occupied room-night against the IQR 23.95-38.19; kg/m2 against the peer set.
hyps.expected: 40.5 kg at 1,000 ft2 per key, 109 at 2,700; crossing 38.19 at about 940 ft2 per key. Refuted if hotel-only GFA is published below that, which no source suggests (most rooms over 570 ft2 before corridors, public space, 43,000 ft2 of events and a 22,000 ft2 spa).

hyps.title: Splitting the single-lot filing into hotel and multifamily raises the hotel's LL97 penalty exposure and lowers the residences', because the hotel floors are more intense per ft2.
hyps.test: residence 1.5-3, assumption knobs): Metric: penalty by component and total.
hyps.expected: total penalty is roughly conserved but shifts to the hotel component; the hotel alone at luxury-peer intensity exceeds its reduced cap by more than the combined lot does. This cannot be settled on current evidence (see H15) but the simulator can show the sensitivity, which is the point: the hotel/residence boundary is a policy and disclosure decision, not a physical one.

hyps.title: Per guest-night the Waldorf's full-scope figure is roughly half the per-room-night figure, and the ratio the Studio uses (1.6 implied) is below the only measured full-service value (1.80-1.92).
hyps.test: Sweep guests per occupied room 1.4-2.0. Metric: per guest-night.
hyps.expected: a 1.6 to 1.86 change moves the guest-night figure by 14%. The food line scales per guest, the building line per room, so the guest-night figure is less sensitive to the ratio under full scope than under energy-only; supported if the Studio shows that asymmetry. Refuted if it does not, which would mean food is not modelled per guest.

hyps.title: Breakfast included in the rate adds 8-30% to an energy-only guest-night depending on the grid, and ADEME's 30% is the low-carbon-grid limit.
hyps.test: Breakfast at 1.3 kg (Filimonau), 3.59 kg (Cool Food threshold) and 5.1 kg (30% of ADEME's 17.11 kg 5-star night, my arithmetic); waste at 0.3 kg per cover disposal-only; energy-only guest-night 28.39 / 1.8 = 15.8 kg.
hyps.expected: +8% to +32% at the 2024-29 factor; the share rises under the 2030 factor; buffet waste adds 0.2 kg disposal-only but 0.6-1.3 kg if the cradle-to-grave factor is wrongly used (I13). Refuted if the Studio's breakfast line falls outside 1-5 kg, which would mean its factor set differs from all three sources.

hyps.title: No single lever reaches the 2030 cap; only a story with electrified heat, a demand reduction of order 30% from the luxury peer EUI, and Zone J RECs for the remainder is compliant in 2030-34, and even that story fails the 2035 cap without further measures.
hyps.test: Baseline: gas boilers plus CHP at luxury peer EUI 135 kBtu/ft2 on 1,666,763 ft2. Stories: (a) electrify 2028 only; (b) electrify plus 30% demand cut; (c) b plus CHPE RECs for the gap; (d) RECs only. Metric: tCO2e against caps 16,450 / 6,420 / 4,400; penalty.
hyps.expected: (a) about 9,560 t in 2030, 49% over; (b) near 6,700 t, marginal; (c) compliant; (d) non-compliant because gas is untouched. In 2035 (cap 4,400) (c) needs either further demand cuts or a lower electricity coefficient that no rule yet provides. Refuted if (a) complies, which would require the heat-pump COP to cut site EUI far below 135, and the Storyline should print the COP that achieves it.

hyps.title: The Waldorf's first LL84 operating year (CY2026) will read 15-20% worse per room-night than steady state because of occupancy ramp, and the per-m2 figure will read close to steady state.
hyps.test: 55-65% in 2026 rising to 76% by 2028, assumption knob): Metric: per room-night and per m2 in 2026 vs 2029.
hyps.expected: per room-night 1.17-1.38x steady state at 65%-55%; per m2 unchanged except for occupancy-dependent loads (DHW, laundry, F&B covers), which CBECS puts at roughly 40% of site energy, so per m2 moves by far less. Supported if the two denominators diverge by that order. Refuted if the Storyline's load model is nearly all occupancy-variable, which the PNNL base load (about 400 kW continuous) argues against.

hyps.title: The Monte Carlo variance of the full-scope guest-night is dominated by the food factor set, not by any amenity assumption.
hyps.test: Ranges from the notes: beef 16.0 (CONCITO, Irish inventory) / 28.73 (Clune) / 99.48 (Poore & Nemecek beef herd) kgCO2e/kg; spa 87-600 kWh/m2 (Bali electric lower bound to TM46); thermal-suite duty 30-100% of nameplate; laundry 4.5-11 kg per room-night; OBC 10.8-26.5%. Metric: variance decomposition of the full-scope guest-night.
hyps.expected: the beef factor alone spans a factor of 6 on the single largest line; amenity ranges span a factor of 7 on lines that are 3-9% of the total. Food wins. Refuted if the Studio's menu composition gives beef a tiny share; the Accor figure (meat 27% of food carbon) argues against that.

hyps.title: The grid-factor choice (eGRID 0.392 vs LL97 0.289) changes the Scope 2 line by 36% and the full-scope total by well under that, and its effect on the F&B share is larger than the effect of any amenity knob.
hyps.test: Metric: Scope 2 line, total, F&B share, under both factors.
hyps.expected: Scope 2 +36%; total +10-20% depending on electricity share; F&B share moves by several points. Supported if the F&B share moves more under the factor toggle than under the spa knob at its full range. This is the test of I1 inside the app.

hyps.title: The hotel-only floor area and the hotel/residence energy split determine both the per-room-night result and the LL97 exposure, and no public record will supply them.

The actual energy of the Guerlain thermal suite (infrared sauna, steam room, hammam, snow cave, cryotherapy chamber) is unknown to within a factor of 3 and the simulator can only propagate the assumed range.
The choice of food emission-factor set (Poore & Nemecek vs Clune vs Agribalyse/CONCITO) moves the headline more than every building lever combined, and only supplier-specific data can resolve it.

insights.title: The F&B share of a hotel footprint is a property of the grid, not the hotel: 48-56% in Zurich, 19% at Accor group level, and it will rise mechanically in New York when the LL97 coefficient halves in 2030
Boundary moves the luxury room-night more than segment does: full-scope is 1.7-2.4x energy-only, while luxury is 2.3x upper-midscale
The denominator reverses the verdict on luxury: 2.55x upper-midscale per room-night, 1.43x per m2, so ~60% of the premium is floor area per key, and the Waldorf is at roughly 2,700 ft2 per key

The hotel/residence single-lot filing makes the LL97 cap and the hotel-only GFA two unknowns with one equation, and the Studio's logged defaults imply a hotel area 2.7 times smaller than the report's bounding case
The 2030 LL97 cliff is a 61% cut in the cap against a 50% cut in the electricity coefficient and a 0% cut in the gas coefficient, so electrification is necessary and not sufficient

Gas heat beats electric resistance today and loses to any heat pump with COP above 1.95 on the eGRID factor, 1.44 on LL97 2024-29 and 0.72 on LL97 2030, so "wait for the grid" has no carbon case in New York
After 2030 a gas CHP cannot beat the LL97 grid coefficient on electricity alone, because it would need 125% electrical efficiency; its entire case rests on recovered heat

Hilton's validated target is absolute (-46.2% Scope 1+2 by 2030 vs 2019), its managed absolute emissions rose from 2.23 to 2.44 Mt between 2008 and 2025, and the 2019 base is undisclosed, so adding a gas-fired flagship is a cost to the target that Hilton's own reporting cannot show

Pool energy is driven by visitors and water, not climate, while every hotel benchmark normalises by climate, so a hotel pool is invisible to the benchmark and the Waldorf's only pool is residents-only

The Waldorf's wellness load is thermal suites with no measured data anywhere, and at the only applicable benchmark the spa is about 2.5 kgCO2e per room-night, 9% of the NYC luxury median, if it is charged to rooms rather than to visits

Claims law closes the offset route on a known date, and the demand-side levers that remain legal move the footprint by low single digits, while the material levers are procurement, electrification and floor area

The largest lines in a legally complete per-stay footprint are the ones no hotel group measures: a return luxury-car airport transfer (about 25.6 kgCO2e) is 90% of the NYC luxury energy-only room-night (28.4)
Counting food waste at cradle-to-grave factors overstates the waste line by 3-7 times and makes a 21% waste cut look like a 21% carbon cut when it is about 4% of food carbon
Occupancy inverts the star ranking and the Waldorf's own pricing works against its per-room-night figure: a 10-point occupancy gap is a 13% change at constant building load
